articles.title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Bolsonaro refuses to accept result: Early analysis from Chatham House experts - Chatham House
articles.summary: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Bolsonaro refuses to accept result: Early analysis from Chatham House experts  Chatham House
articles.full_text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, has been re-elected president of Brazil for a fourth term. Lula secured 51.79 per cent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent.
The victory was a surprise: Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, led in the first round of the election held on 4 October. The result was announced after an unusual decision on Sunday by the country’s Supreme Court, which allowed polling centres to remain open longer than planned.
‘This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country’.
Defeated candidate Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, saying:
‘It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded.’
Below, Chatham House experts provide analysis of the meaning of the result for Brazilians, the region and the world.
1.    Dr Christopher Sabatini on what next for US relations?
2.    Dr Bruno Binetti on Brazil’s China policy
3.    Vanessa Rubio Marquez on the left and right in Latin America
4.    Luis Miguel Castilla Rubio on Lula’s policies and Brazil’s economy
What next for US relations?
Christopher Sabatini, Director of Chatham House’s Latin America Programme
As many waited for the administration of President Donald Trump to recognize President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s unexpected second-round presidential victory, other heads of state rushed to congratulate the Workers’ Party president’s victory over conservative Flávio Bolsonaro.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney all publicly congratulated Lula on his victory. Even Brazil’s more conservative neighbours joined the chorus, including Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, Chilean President José Antonio Kast, and Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.
The White House’s hesitation is not surprising. It had been counting on the election of Bolsonaro to complete its bingo card of right-wing presidents in the Western Hemisphere, following a period of sustained electoral success for right-wing candidates stretching from Honduras to Argentina. But Latin American regional solidarity and respect for democratic institutions and the popular will trumped ideology and alignment with the US.
Adding Latin America’s largest democracy and economy would have represented a major victory for the self-proclaimed ‘Donroe Doctrine’. Instead, public support for Lula’s re-election may demonstrate that the bloc of Trump-aligned and Trump-adjacent presidents may not be as strong and ideological as many thought. (Only Argentine President Javier Milei has withheld congratulations for Lula.)
Meanwhile, Flávio continues to call for the annulment of the elections, claiming fraud – much as his father, Jair, did in 2022 when he lost to Lula. Part of his claim hinges on a Supreme Court justice who supported Lula’s Workers’ Party request to extend voting by two hours on Sunday.
That request was made originally by both parties to Brazil’s electoral court – in order to accommodate voters who struggled to make it to the booths due to heavy rains, and others allegedly affected by limited public transportation. But the decision to kick the request up to the Supreme Court after the electoral court failed to respond casts a pall over the results – and further threatens the reputation of a Supreme Court already under suspicion for being politicized.
Brazil’s modern, transparent voting system will be able to demonstrate the results – for those who want to believe them. But for core Bolsonaro supporters, trusting the results may be difficult. Flávio’s father also claimed unproven fraud in 2022. And father and son have baked distrust of the judicial and electoral system into their political DNA, polarizing politics and society in Brazil.
In the end, how far Flávio’s team decides to take its claims of fraud may depend on the White House and the US State Department. Both had a lot riding on a Bolsonaro victory. For Trump it would have been the crowning achievement for his support in the region, during this heavy year of presidential elections across the hemisphere.
For others the issue is more ideological and personal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, like many Cuban-Americans, saw Lula’s Workers’ Party as complicit in upholding the communist regimes in Cuba and Nicaragua. Creating a ring of conservative, anti-communist governments across the hemisphere to stand with the US against those regimes has long been a dream of Republican administrations and Cuban-Americans in Florida. Their perspective will likely also help decide whether and when the Trump administration accepts a Lula victory.
With conservative majorities in both houses of Congress, Lula will have a difficult time attempting to tackle the economic and fiscal reforms necessary to keep the government solvent and address its looming sovereign debt. But the biggest loser in the election is social trust. The country’s voters are now almost evenly split between Bolsonaro and Lula (only 3.6 per cent separated the two leaders). And popular confidence in the Supreme Court may decline even more.
Will Lula change Brazil’s approach to China?
Bruno Binetti, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme
Lula’s re-election, following a campaign in which he declared that Brazil was ‘nobody’s backyard’ and denounced foreign interference, will be welcomed in Beijing.
China retains a close partner in Latin America’s largest economy, at a time when most countries in the region have moved closer to the Trump administration. Lula shares China’s commitment to a multipolar international order with a stronger role for the Global South. That includes efforts within BRICS to reduce reliance on the US dollar in international trade, reform global financial institutions and expand climate finance for developing countries.
This partnership is underpinned by strong economic ties – ties so important they would have endured a Bolsonaro victory. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, driven by Brazilian exports of soybeans, iron ore and crude oil. In 2025, Brazilian exports to China reached $100 billion, compared with $38 billion to the US. This makes continued engagement with Beijing a priority for the powerful agribusiness sector, which is well represented in Congress and traditionally aligned with Bolsonaro and the political right.
Brazil was also the world’s largest recipient of Chinese investment in 2025, with Chinese firms expanding their presence in electricity infrastructure, manufacturing and mining. In the automotive sector, BYD and Great Wall Motor have established electric vehicle production facilities in Brazil, and Lula is pushing Chinese manufacturers to use more local suppliers and create jobs.
Brazil-China relations are likely to deepen during Lula’s fourth term, especially if the Trump administration continues to impose tariffs and other trade restrictions on Brazil.
Yet Lula is the ultimate pragmatist. He has always sought to maintain good relations with competing powers. Brazil and the US are already discussing a potential trade agreement that could include cooperation on critical minerals, a top priority for Washington as it tries to reduce dependence on China.
With the world’s second-largest rare-earth reserves, Lula is open to investment from both China and the US, provided it helps Brazil develop its own processing industries and move up the value chain,
What does this result mean for the left and right in Latin America?
Vanessa Rubio Marquez, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme
With Lula’s clear victory in the presidential run-off on 25 October, the two largest Latin American economies, Brazil and Mexico, will be perceived as the remaining guardians of the left, in a region that has largely flipped to the right of the political spectrum in recent years. However, the more relevant question is whether being left or right in the Western Hemisphere – and the world – still means what it once did.
Traditionally, the distinction between left and right was relatively clear. The left favoured a stronger role for the state in reducing inequality and redistributing wealth. The right, by contrast, placed greater emphasis on individual responsibility, private enterprise and preserving existing economic and social structures, accepting inequalities as a natural feature of society.
Today, these boundaries are being blurred. For instance, under Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil increased minimum monthly welfare transfers by 50 per cent (R$400 to R$600), reaching over 20 million families ahead of the 2022 election. And the reduction of the working week from 44 to 40 hours also took place under his mandate. Similar measures to protect specific sectors in society were implemented in Ecuador, where right-wing Daniel Noboa introduced financial assistance for vulnerable entrepreneurs.
However, the left -wing Mexican government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador limited pandemic spending and direct budget support to 0.7 per cent of GDP, compared with over 3 per cent across G20 emerging economies. And Chile’s left-wing president, Gabriel Boric, oversaw a 23.1 per cent real reduction in government spending in 2022.
Ever more, the extremes of left and right converge in pragmatic, immediate and populist policies. The more important divide is how governments exercise power, respect democratic institutions and protect individual freedoms while they deliver for the people.
A very interesting case of a tension between democracy and tangible results in matters that people prioritise is seen in El Salvador. President Nayib Bukele’s crackdown on gangs has brought major security gains, but at a cost to civil liberties. Emergency powers have been extended 55 times since 2022, with over 93,000 arrests and restrictions on due process.

articles.title: Lula's reelection expected to bring continuity to China-Brazil ties, fresh momentum for Global South cooperation: expert - Global Times
articles.summary: Lula's reelection expected to bring continuity to China-Brazil ties, fresh momentum for Global South cooperation: expert  Global Times
articles.full_text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (center) delivers a speech after winning the election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Photo: VCG
"Thank you, Brazilian people," Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva wrote on social media on Sunday night after securing a historic fourth presidential term in a dramatic electoral comeback.
When asked to comment on Lula's reelection victory and China's expectations for bilateral ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that China takes note of the announcement by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court of President Lula's runoff victory and extends congratulations on that. China stands ready to work with Brazil to advance the building of the China-Brazil community with a shared future, he noted. 
Lula's victory has drawn international attention not only for its implications for Latin America's shifting political landscape, but also for the future of China-Brazil relations, with prospects for deeper economic cooperation, sustained high-level diplomatic engagement and closer coordination within BRICS and other multilateral frameworks coming into focus.
With 99.96 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.78 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.22 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally reported by Xinhua News Agency.
Lula will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, for a four-year term, marking his fourth election as Brazil's president.
The victory marked the first time a presidential candidate in Brazil had overturned a first-round deficit to win a runoff election. According to Xinhua, Brazil's presidential election follows a two-round majoritarian system. To win in the first round, held on October 4, a candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes. Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent. As neither candidate crossed the 50-percent threshold, the two advanced to a runoff, which Lula won.
The election outcome comes amid significant political shifts across Latin America and growing geopolitical competition in the region. International media have highlighted the implications of Lula's victory for Brazil's relations with major powers, particularly China and the US, as well as the country's role in promoting cooperation among Global South nations.
The South China Morning Post reported on Monday that Lula's reelection would extend the tenure of an administration under which Chinese investment in Brazil had reached record levels. 
Pan Deng, director of the Latin America and Caribbean Region Law Center at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection has provided stability and predictability for China-Brazil relations over the next four years.
Pan said the political consensus reached by the two countries' leaders during Lula's 2023 visit to China, together with sustained high-level exchanges, has strengthened mutual trust and provided strategic guidance for bilateral ties. Despite potential constraints from a conservative Congress, cooperation with China enjoys broad support across Brazil's political spectrum and is unlikely to be significantly affected by domestic political divisions, he added.
China's top diplomat Wang Yi met with Special Advisor to the President of Brazil Celso Amorim on September 16 in Beijing. Amorim said Brazil stands ready to work with China to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state and inject new connotations into building a Brazil-China community with a shared future for a more just world and a more sustainable planet, Xinhua reported.
China has remained Brazil's largest trading partner for years, with bilateral economic ties forming a major pillar of the broader relationship.
Trade between Brazil and China reached a record $143.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026, reinforcing China's position as Brazil's largest trading partner. Brazilian exports to the Chinese market totaled $84.7 billion between January and September, an increase of 12 percent compared with the same period in 2025. Imports from China rose 9.9 percent to $58.6 billion.
The figures were released by Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services and compiled by the Brazil-China Business Council, according to a report published by Valor Econômico and covered by Brasil 247.
Looking ahead, Pan identified three areas with significant growth potential for China-Brazil cooperation: green and low-carbon development, including renewable energy and environmental protection; the digital economy and artificial intelligence, particularly in agriculture and AI governance; and expanded aerospace cooperation, building on the two countries' longstanding satellite partnership to advance remote-sensing applications in agriculture, disaster prevention and logistics.
Xu Shicheng, vice president of the China Society of Latin American Studies, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection could also help take China-Brazil relations to a new level, as bilateral cooperation has expanded beyond traditional commodity trade into emerging sectors such as electric vehicles, renewable energy, infrastructure and advanced technologies.
Beyond specific industries, Chinese analysts also pointed out that the Lula administration's emphasis on strategic autonomy and economic development aimed at improving people's livelihoods aligns closely with China's pursuit of high-quality development and open, inclusive international cooperation. At the multilateral level, Lula's reelection is also expected to provide continuity for Brazil's participation in BRICS and broader Global South cooperation, they noted.
China and Brazil could continue coordinating their positions on reform of the United Nations and World Trade Organization, global debt restructuring and international climate negotiations, helping ensure that global governance arrangements better reflect the concerns and development needs of emerging economies, Pan said.
The two countries could also jointly initiate inclusive cooperation projects targeting developing nations, providing additional opportunities for Global South countries to participate in international economic and technological cooperation. Pan said such initiatives could contribute to a more equitable international development environment and strengthen the collective voice of developing countries in global affairs.
The election has also attracted attention for its potential implications for Latin America's political landscape.
Reuters reported that Lula's victory came against the backdrop of recent electoral gains by right-wing political forces in several Latin American countries, raising questions about how Brazil's regional diplomacy might evolve during his next term.
Pan argued that Lula's victory should not simply be viewed as a return of a particular ideological camp, but rather as a pragmatic response by Brazilian voters to economic and social challenges, including high inflation and poverty pressures associated with neoliberal policies. The outcome could strengthen Latin America's pursuit of independent development and inject fresh momentum into regional integration, he said.
Xu noted that Lula could face considerable domestic political challenges during his fourth term, as right-wing and center-right forces secured significant representation in Brazil's Congress. Nevertheless, he said Lula's previous poverty alleviation and social welfare policies have retained support among lower-income voters, while his administration is expected to continue prioritizing BRICS cooperation and Brazil's role in the Global South.
The election also sends a message that Latin American countries can pursue development paths suited to their own national conditions rather than relying on Western-led models, while expanding diversified international partnerships, Pan said. He added that the result reflects growing regional aspirations for independent decision-making and resistance to external interference.

articles.title: Brazil draws record Chinese investment. Is Lula’s industrial strategy a problem? - South China Morning Post
articles.summary: Brazil draws record Chinese investment. Is Lula’s industrial strategy a problem?  South China Morning Post
articles.full_text:
The re-elected leader has championed closer economic ties with Beijing but also wants his nation to move up the value chain
China and Brazil are expected to sustain close economic ties following the re-election of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as president, though his push to strengthen domestic industry and production could complicate the outlook for Chinese companies operating in Latin America’s largest economy, analysts said.
Lula defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s run-off election, securing a fourth, non-consecutive term. Following his victory, Lula told reporters and allies at a hotel in Sao Paulo that “Brazil refuses to be anyone’s backyard” – a remark widely seen as a pointed message to Washington.
Chen Fengying, a researcher at the Beijing-based China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, said Lula’s plans to diversify Brazil’s international partnerships and maintain strategic autonomy from the United States could create opportunities for Beijing. Chinese investment, she added, could also help Brazil upgrade its economy.

articles.title: How will the US midterm elections impact policies toward South Korea and North Korea? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: How will the US midterm elections impact policies toward South Korea and North Korea?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The US midterm elections are unlikely to fundamentally alter Washington's policy toward the US-South Korea alliance, but they could affect President Donald Trump's demands on security, trade, and efforts to resume dialogue with North Korea. This is the assessment of experts studying the Korean Peninsula.
According to Yonhap news agency, experts in Washington generally believe that U.S. policy toward the Korean Peninsula will not change significantly, regardless of the election results. However, the situation in Congress could impact the level of government oversight, bilateral economic relations, and the impetus for President Trump to seek a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Ellen Kim, a senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute (KEI), believes the election results are likely to have only a limited impact on US-South Korea relations. However, if the Democratic Party gains more seats, it could increase its scrutiny of the Trump administration's policies.
Kim said, "The election results are likely to have only a limited impact on U.S.- South Korea bilateral issues."
According to this expert, if the Democratic Party wins, the US Congress could more closely monitor the policies of the Trump administration, including tariffs and security issues such as US-South Korea civilian nuclear cooperation and the nuclear-powered submarine program.
Robert Rapson, former US chargé d'affaires ad interim in Seoul, warned that the US-South Korea alliance could continue to face instability due to President Trump's transactional foreign policy approach, regardless of the election results.
Rapson stated, "This is likely to cause the U.S.-South Korea alliance to continue experiencing periods of instability." According to Rapson, the increasingly diverse bilateral issues require both governments to handle their relationship cautiously.
Meanwhile, Andrew Yeo, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute, suggests that if Republicans lose seats, Congress could restrict President Trump's scope of action through oversight, legislative decisions, and budgetary controls. However, this scenario is unlikely to lead to a major shift in Washington's policy toward South Korea.
Yeo pointed out several issues that could put pressure on the alliance – including tariffs, defense cost-sharing, disagreements in intelligence, and policy coordination on the Middle East. According to him, the evolution of bilateral relations will largely depend on the decisions of President Trump and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung.
Intelligence relations between the two countries have shown signs of strain after South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly disclosed information about a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong in March.
Yeo also warned of the risk that Washington could make decisions that would exclude Seoul from the diplomatic process with Pyongyang, or adjust military exercises and troop deployments in a way that could diminish deterrence capabilities.

According to Scott Snyder, President and CEO of KEI, the election results are less important than South Korea's ability to align its priorities with President Trump's agenda and capture the attention of the American leader amidst Washington's numerous international crises.
Snyder emphasized, "South Korea's ability to capture President Trump's time and attention will be the most important factor shaping U.S.-South Korea relations."
Regarding trade and investment, Yeo suggested that if the Republican Party loses, President Trump might reduce pressure on South Korea to invest in the US. Conversely, if the Republican Party wins, he might increase demands for Seoul to invest more in the US semiconductor industry.
Ms. Kim noted that the majority of trade authority rests with the executive branch, making it difficult for Congress to reverse the Trump administration's tariff policies, even if the Democrats gain control of one or both houses.
According to her, efforts to oppose Trump's tariff policies through legislation could also face obstacles, as Congress needs enough votes to override the president's veto.
Offering a different perspective, Patrick Cronin, chairman of the Asia-Pacific security research program at the Hudson Institute, suggested that Democratic control of Congress could help stabilize the US-South Korea alliance and encourage President Trump to pursue bilateral investment initiatives.
Cronin commented: "Democratic control of Congress could help stabilize the coalition and encourage President Trump to fulfill his commitments in an area where he can claim success, such as attracting unprecedented investments in energy, shipbuilding, and other industries."
Regarding North Korea, some experts believe that the results of the US midterm elections could affect the impetus for President Trump to resume dialogue with leader Kim Jong-un. However, the prospect of substantive negotiations still largely depends on whether Pyongyang is willing to participate.
Ellen Kim believes that if the Republican Party loses seats, President Trump may seek to achieve more foreign policy successes, thereby paying more attention to resuming contact with North Korea.
"A defeat in the midterm elections could make President Trump even more eager to achieve a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea," she said.
According to her, Pyongyang will closely monitor whether Washington is willing to make concessions to facilitate the resumption of negotiations.

Rapson suggested that President Trump's desire to resolve outstanding diplomatic issues with North Korea is likely to remain, regardless of the election results, unless major political upheaval occurs. He also predicted that the US leader will continue to be interested in the possibility of holding a summit with Kim in 2027, even if the two sides do not meet during Trump's Asia trip next month.
According to Yeo, the results of the midterm elections are unlikely to determine whether a Trump-Kim summit will take place. The key factor is the North Korean leader's assessment of the appropriate time to resume dialogue.
Meanwhile, Cronin suggested that a shift in congressional control could prompt President Trump to focus more on foreign policy. However, increased congressional oversight could also narrow his ability to make significant concessions in negotiations with Pyongyang.
"Therefore, even if President Trump succeeds in resuming high-level talks with Kim Jong-un, the room for him to make substantive policy changes is likely to remain limited," Cronin stated.
According to this expert, easing US sanctions or withdrawing US forces from South Korea are not easy steps to take.
